checks.note: The text says all integers are rational because they can be written over 1, and the exercise has the student state natural, whole or integer for a rational number. Both use the classification in 1-1.
Both texts explain how to pick the multiplier from the number of recurring digits. Neither mentions or uses dot/bar notation, so reliance on 1-3 is not shown.
The text only says recurring decimals need more work than the other case. It does not show the place-value denominator method being reused.
WE4 first writes 120/99 as a recurring decimal in dot notation, then rounds it. Writing a fraction as a decimal is a step in the rounding.
Part (a) rounds i to 2 decimal places, and part (b) calculates A from that rounded value. Rounding is a step in the dst task.
The text only defines a surd as an nth root that is not a rational number. Locating a surd between consecutive integers is not shown to depend on classifying rational versus irrational.
Neither text recalls the consecutive-integers method. The intro only notes that sqrt3 lies above 1 and below 2, and does not say 1-decimal estimation builds on that.
The ranking exercise and the intro do not state that ranking uses the between-consecutive-integers skill. The dependence is plausible but not shown.
Ex 3g, 2(3x+y)(3x-y)-(3x-y)^2, needs a constant times a binomial and the difference of products. WE8 distributes each term of one bracket over the other.
The binomial-times-trinomial rule is written as A(C+D+E)+B(C+D+E), and WE9 uses x(...)-1(...). Each step is a monomial or constant times a trinomial.
Both products start with (3x+2)(3x-2) or (2a-b)(2a+b), a difference of squares from 1-2. The result is then multiplied by a further factor.
Ex 4 expands (x+b)(x-1) and matches coefficients. Ex 7b is a squared-binomial expansion that finds the value without solving for x.
Part (b) expands a binomial times a trinomial, giving a^3+1/(27a^3). Part (c) then finds that value without solving for a.
The text defines factorisation as the reverse of expanding and recalls 2(x+1)=2x+2, a constant times a binomial.
The text says it has already seen (ax+b)(ax-b) expand to a^2x^2-b^2, then reverses it to factorise.
The text calls common factors the starting point of all factorisation, and WE12 takes out the common factor to finish the grouping.
WE12 takes out the common binomial factor, for example 7(x+2y)+b(x+2y)=(x+2y)(7+b). That is the 1-2 method used as the grouping step.
WE11 and Ex 6:2 take out the common binomial factor, for example (a^2-4)(3a-7), before factorising the difference of squares.
16k^2-4 needs a common factor of 4 taken out first. The text calls common factors the starting point of all factorisation.
The text frames factorising a quadratic as the opposite of multiplying two binomials, and expands each bracket pair to find the middle term.
The method has the student expand all options to find the correct middle term. WE13 checks by multiplying the factors.
The cube identities are called results of multiplying a binomial and a trinomial. WE14 expands (a-1)(a^2+a+1) to check the factorisation.
WE18 takes out the common factor in the denominator. The text says the different factorisation methods are applied to the numerator and denominator.
WE18 says to use grouping to factorise the numerator before cancelling.
WE19 has the denominator x^2-4 factorised as a difference of squares. Ex 1j, (9x^2-16)/(6x-8), also needs a difference of squares.
WE19 factorises x^2-x-2 in the numerator. Ex 1m, (x^2-2x-15)/(5x-25), needs a factorised trinomial.
Ex 1r and Ex 1s have numerators 6a^2-7a-3 and 2x^2-x-1, which are trinomials with a not equal to 1. They must be factorised before simplifying.
WE21 factorises x^3-1 in a denominator, and Ex 1o has a denominator x^3-27. Both need the cube identity.
WE19 factorises the numerator and denominator, changes the division to multiplication by the reciprocal, and cancels. That is the 8-1-1 simplification used within a product or quotient.
WE20 factorises the denominators first. WE21 also cancels a common factor, (x^2+x+1)/((x-1)(x^2+x+1)), while combining fractions.
